label: When You Are Facing Death
framing: Scripture does not pretend death is nothing. It calls death an enemy, the last one. But it announces over that enemy a stranger thing still, that Christ has gone through death ahead of you and come out the other side, so that for those who are his the grave is a passage and not a wall.
cultural: The ancient world feared death as a shadowy nothing, and even Israel long spoke of the grave as silence. Into that, the resurrection of Jesus landed as scandal and shock, an empty tomb that rewrote what death could mean. The early Christians faced execution with a calm that baffled Rome, because they were sure of a life on the far side of dying.
historical: The church developed an entire art of dying well, the ars moriendi of the late medieval period, teaching believers to face the end with honesty and hope rather than terror. From the martyrs who sang at the stake to the modern hospice movement, founded by the Christian physician Cicely Saunders in 1967, the church has insisted that the dying be accompanied, not abandoned.
application: Speak openly about what you face, with God and with the people you love, rather than facing it alone behind a brave mask. Put your affairs and your relationships in order, say the words that need saying, and make peace where you can. Lean on hospice and palliative care, your medical team, and a pastor, for the dying deserve comfort and company. And rest your hope not in your own strength but in the One who has already passed through death for you.

verses.text: Now since the children have flesh and blood, He too shared in their humanity, so that by His death He might destroy him who holds the power of death, that is, the devil, and free those who all their lives were held in slavery by their fear of death.
verses.where: Hebrews explains why the Son of God took on flesh and blood: so that through his own death he might break the power of the one who holds the power of death, and free those who all their lives were held in slavery by the fear of death. Scripture takes that fear seriously. It does not shame it; it says Christ came to set people free from it.

verses.text: Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for You are with me; Your rod and Your staff, they comfort me.
verses.where: David's shepherd psalm does not skip the valley of the shadow of death; it walks straight through it. The comfort is not that the sheep will be spared the valley but that the shepherd will be with it there. The site's note puts it plainly: the promise is not you will not go into the valley, but you are with me in it.

verses.text: Remember Him before the silver cord is snapped and the golden bowl is crushed, before the pitcher is shattered at the spring and the wheel is broken at the well, before the dust returns to the ground from which it came and the spirit returns to God who gave it.
verses.where: The Teacher ends his poem on old age with a house falling silent and a lamp shattered: the dust returns to the ground it came from, and the spirit returns to God who gave it. Scripture is honest about what happens to the body. It is just as clear that the person goes back to the one who made them.

verses.text: Then he said, “Jesus, remember me when You come into Your kingdom!” And Jesus said to him, “Truly I tell you, today you will be with Me in Paradise.”
verses.where: One of the criminals crucified beside Jesus asks only to be remembered when Jesus comes into his kingdom. Jesus answers with more than he asked: today you will be with me in Paradise. A man with nothing to offer and hours to live is promised the company of Christ.

verses.text: Then Jesus called out in a loud voice, “Father, into Your hands I commit My Spirit.” And when He had said this, He breathed His last.
verses.where: Jesus dies praying the words of Psalm 31, committing his spirit into his Father's hands. The verb is the one used for leaving something valuable with a trusted keeper. The last word of his earthly life is Father, and he gives Christians words to die with.

verses.text: While they were stoning him, Stephen appealed, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.” Falling on his knees, he cried out in a loud voice, “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.” And when he had said this, he fell asleep.
verses.where: Stephen, the first person killed for following Jesus, sees Jesus standing at God's right hand as the stones fall. He prays, Lord Jesus, receive my spirit, and then asks that the sin not be held against those killing him. He dies as his Lord died, trusting and forgiving.

verses.text: If we live, we live to the Lord, and if we die, we die to the Lord. So whether we live or die, we belong to the Lord.
verses.where: In a chapter about believers who disagree over food and days, Paul sets down the one thing they share: none of us lives or dies to himself. If we live, we live to the Lord; if we die, we die to the Lord. Christ died and rose so that he might be Lord of the dead and the living.

verses.text: Therefore we are always confident, although we know that while we are at home in the body, we are away from the Lord. For we walk by faith, not by sight. We are confident, then, and would prefer to be away from the body and at home with the Lord.
verses.where: Paul calls the body a tent that will be taken down, and he groans for the house God has prepared. He would rather be away from the body and at home with the Lord. The site's note says that every Christian tradition holds to this comfort in some way, while Christians read the details of what happens before the resurrection differently.

verses.text: “Where, O Death, is your victory? Where, O Death, is your sting?” The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law. But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ!
verses.where: Paul ends his long chapter on the resurrection by taunting death in the words of Hosea: where, O death, is your victory, where is your sting? Then he names the sting, sin, and gives thanks to God, who gives the victory through Jesus Christ. The same chapter has already called death an enemy; the taunt is a promise about its end, not a denial that it hurts now.

verses.text: And I heard a voice from heaven telling me to write, “Blessed are the dead—those who die in the Lord from this moment on.” “Yes,” says the Spirit, “they will rest from their labors, for their deeds will follow them.”
verses.where: In the middle of visions of judgment, John hears a voice from heaven telling him to write: blessed are the dead who die in the Lord from now on. The Spirit adds that they will rest from their labors, for their deeds will follow them. Death in the Lord is called rest, and nothing done for him is lost.

whole: If fear or grief about dying has become more than you can carry, or you feel you do not want to go on, please tell someone, a pastor, a friend, a doctor or a counselor; you do not have to carry it alone, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn. Everyone faces death, and most people spend their lives not looking at it. Then something brings it close: age, an illness, the death of someone near, a close call. People describe fear of pain, fear of being a burden, fear of the unknown, regret over what has not been done or said, and grief at leaving the people they love. Some feel that a Christian ought not to be afraid, and so they carry the fear in secret.

Scripture is honest about death in every direction. It says the dust returns to the ground and the spirit to God who gave it. It calls death an enemy, the last one. It records that Jesus himself, facing death, was in anguish. And it names the fear of death as a kind of slavery that has held people all their lives, which is exactly why the Son of God took on flesh and blood and died: to break the power of death and set people free from that fear. The Christian answer to the fear of death is not to pretend death is nothing. It is a person who went through it first.

That is why Christians have long spoken of learning to die well. It is less a technique than a way of trusting. It means saying what needs to be said, to God and to the people you love, while you can: thanks, love, apology, forgiveness. It means setting your affairs in order so that others are not left with confusion. It means letting the church be near, through prayer, Scripture read aloud, the Lord's Supper, and simple presence, and letting a pastor know you. It means bringing the fear itself to God rather than hiding it, as the psalmist did in the valley and as Jesus did in the garden. And it means learning the prayers Christians have died with: into your hands I commit my spirit, Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.

The hope Scripture gives is not a soft one. The criminal on the cross was promised, that same day, the company of Christ. Paul said that to be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord. The dead who die in the Lord are called blessed, and they rest. And beyond that rest lies the resurrection, when the last enemy is destroyed and the body itself is raised. None of us lives or dies to himself; whether we live or die, we are the Lord's. That does not make dying easy. It means you do not walk into the valley alone, and that the one who walks with you has already come out the other side.
deep.sit: What would you want to have said, or set right, if you knew your time was short, and what keeps you from doing it now?

prayer.lead: David's confidence that God will not abandon him to the grave, and that in God's presence is fullness of joy. Pray it slowly, even if the confidence is not yet yours.
prayer.text: Therefore my heart is glad and my tongue rejoices; my body also will dwell securely. For You will not abandon my soul to Sheol, nor will You let Your Holy One see decay. You have made known to me the path of life; You will fill me with joy in Your presence, with eternal pleasures at Your right hand.

careLines.text: If your grief is so heavy that you cannot carry it, or you feel you do not want to go on, please tell someone: a pastor, a friend, a doctor or a counsellor.
You do not have to carry it alone.
Grief and hope can live in the same heart.
The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
